correctness.rationale: Simplex-volume inclusion–exclusion gives the exact joint maximum--one-threshold event probability and the displayed piecewise polynomial covariance, with all integration limits handled explicitly. Conditioning on one coordinate yields the convex function g(x)=E max(x,(1-x)Q), whose two crossings with E M force C(t) to decrease, increase, then decrease; boundary values C(0)=C(1)=0 imply exactly one interior zero. Exact evaluation at t=1/m and positive association of M with its own upper-tail event at t=1/2 establish sharp brackets. Exact Fraction tests (539) and independent conditional-integral comparisons (44) plus 10 numerical roots corroborate the argument, without being substituted for its infinite quantifiers.

originality.rationale: The inspected complete preprints by Schlemm (2014, arXiv:1405.6114) and Bose–Dasgupta–Maulik (2008, arXiv:0803.3518) give marginal maximum-spacing moments and maximum laws, not the mixed maximum--threshold-count covariance or its one-switch sign theorem. Earlier random-spacing references address distributions and random divisions of an interval; their inaccessible full texts leave a real residual prior-coverage risk. A semantic result index yielded nearby results for nested exceedance counts and other gap functionals, but those claims neither imply the present joint regression sign law nor use the maximum statistic. This is a best-knowledge scientific originality assessment rather than a proof of global priority.
residual_risks: Older complete surveys and stick-breaking papers could contain a broader joint-moment identity from which this covariance follows; their full texts were inaccessible.
Semantic search and comparisons of named nearby results do not exhaust all publications or establish global novelty.
The theorem is restricted to uniform-simplex spacings and does not cover general Dirichlet or independently normalized gaps.

value.rationale: Maximum gap and number of gaps above a resolution threshold are two canonical multiscale random-spacing statistics. Although the exceedance statistic itself defines the event of a large maximum, their covariance is negative at fine thresholds because of the fixed-total-length constraint; for coarse thresholds it is positive. An exact sign-switch classification for every dimension, including a sharp universal bracket and a closed finite-sample formula, distinguishes the dependence structure and informs interpretation of joint extreme/spacing diagnostics. Neither marginal maximum formulas nor a nested-count covariance resolves this mixed-sign phenomenon.
